title: Nordest’s First 32” Gravel Bike: The Arisco Ti
content:
The Nordest Arisco Ti, the Portuguese brand’s first 32er gravel bike, is designed for long rides on rough terrain. It’s attractively simple and meant to last the long haul.

The Arisco Ti was born for terrain that neither forgives nor asks permission: tracks between hillside and broken tarmac, trails that change mood with the season, surfaces that demand the bike, and whoever rides it, adapt rather than impose. The name isn’t decoration. It’s a statement of intent: this bike doesn’t take kindly to being tamed. And that’s the fun of it.

Arisco Ti Quick Hits

  • Wheels 32″ up to 2.4″
  • Frame Ti3Al2.5V double-butted
  • 68mm T47 bottom bracket
  • BOOST rear axle with interchangeable dropouts.
  • Compatible with SRAM UDH Full Mount rear derailleur
  • Eyelets on seat stays for rear rack
  • 34.9mm seatpost clamp included
  • TR44 head tube fro ZS44/EC44 headset type
  • For 31.6mm seatpost
  • Compatible with internal dropper seatpost control
  • Weight for M/L size: 1.950 g.
  • Thru Axle, seat clamp and dropouts included with the frame
  • Forks 444mm A-C with 60mm offset
  • Frameset only
  • MSRP: 1.899,00 € – 1.999,00 € ($2,082.01 – $2,194.72 USD)

An Explosive Cocktail

468 mm chainstays, ultra-short for a 32er, with clearance for tyres up to 2.4″ and a 76º seat tube angle, so you climb like you’re late for lunch. An extra-long top tube, 70 mm stem and 68º head tube angle, paired with a 444 mm fork, so you descend grinning from ear to ear.

The result is a bike that’s as much fun on your local loop as on the trip of your dreams. Load up your bikepacking bags or panniers: the seatstays have rack mounts, so “it won’t fit” is no longer an excuse.

Arisco (Trás-os-Montes dialect)

n./adj. A rustic inhabitant with a deep knowledge of the mountain paths, who lives in harmony with rugged nature and shies away from company.

Arisco is the silence between two villages separated by a hill nobody crosses without need. It is the passing of the wolf, sensed but never seen, the shadow that crosses the stone path as evening falls. It is the character of a land that doesn’t give itself up easily: granite that won’t be worked without effort, the winter wind that slips through the cracks of the stone houses without asking permission.

In Trás-os-Montes, arisco isn’t hostile: it’s reserved. It is the wise wariness of those who have learned, generation after generation, that not everything deserves to be tamed. The fox that flees before it is seen. The shepherd who says little but looks long. The village that clings to the mountainside as if afraid the plain might carry it away.

It is also the language itself: rough, short words that aren’t polished to sound pretty; they are said because they need saying, and that’s that. A vocabulary that has survived arisco, resisting disappearance for centuries, hidden in the valleys of the Douro and the Sabor, where nobody came looking until it was almost too late.

To be arisco, in this land, is not a flaw. It is a form of loyalty: to what is one’s own, to what is hard, to what doesn’t readily yield to those who come from outside. It is the memory of a territory that learned, among wolves and stone, that the wild that is well kept has no need to apologize for being so.
